shows.title: Changing Unchanging (변하는 변하지 않는)
shows.description:
Timed to the third anniversary of Park Seo-Bo's death, this retrospective spreads forty works across Kukje's K1 and K3 galleries and its hanok, tracing more than five decades of the artist's Écriture (myobop) practice — a title that literally means "a way of drawing as though writing." Park was one of the founding figures of Dansaekhwa, the monochrome painting movement that reshaped how Korean abstraction was understood internationally, and the Écriture series is the clearest record of how he pursued that idea: repeated pencil lines pulled through wet white pigment starting in 1967, later opening up to hanji paper, ink and color.

The show's title captures a real tension in how Park is remembered. His relationship to Korea's democratic movement was contested enough that the Gwangju Biennale dropped a prize named for him a few months before his death, yet the work itself has only grown more central to how Dansaekhwa gets told internationally, including a late run of "Newspaper Ecriture" pieces where he scored and splattered oil paint over old copies of Le Monde — turning printed records of political struggle into a private, repetitive gesture. Following the concurrent opening of the Park Seo-Bo Museum near his former studio, this is the larger of two anniversary presentations and the fuller survey of how the Écriture idea evolved across a lifetime of repetition.

For anyone trying to understand Dansaekhwa beyond the market narrative that's built up around it in the past decade, this is as thorough a chance as any to see the range of Park's mark-making in one place — from the pared-back white paintings of the 1970s through the more chromatic, textured late work.

shows.title: Pictos and Pitwall (핏월과 픽토)
shows.description:
Seeun Kim borrows her two organizing terms from Formula 1 racing and traffic signage: the "pit wall," the command center where split-second strategic calls get made during a race, and "picto," shorthand for the pictograms that compress complex information into instantly legible symbols. Both are systems built to process speed and risk faster than an individual body can — and Kim's paintings are an attempt to register what it feels like to live inside built environments that constantly renew their own rules faster than any one person can track them.

The paintings translate those systems into a sensory, sometimes opaque painterly language rather than illustrating them directly, using the body that paints as the actual site where the city's shifting states get processed. The installation itself extends the point: Kim's works spread from K2's second floor down to the ground floor and out into the gallery's courtyard, so the physical act of moving through the show mimics the disorientation the paintings are about.

It's a good pairing with the concurrent Park Seo-Bo retrospective a floor away — one show about the accumulation of a single repeated gesture over fifty years, the other about the overload of information in real time — and worth seeing as a snapshot of where a younger generation of Korean painters is taking abstraction next.

shows.title: reimagine Yun Hyong-keun
shows.description:
Spread across PKM's main gallery and its PKM+ annex, this is a thirty-work survey of Yun Hyong-keun, one of the defining figures of Korean Dansaekhwa monochrome painting, timed to coincide with the public opening of the Seogyo-dong house where he lived and worked. It traces his career in two distinct movements: the main gallery holds the large 1970s through early-1990s Cheonjimun ("Heaven and Earth Gate") paintings, built from a restrained palette of layered blue and burnt umber pigment that rises in columnar forms on either side of the canvas, leaving an open channel of raw linen between them. The annex takes up the work after Yun's pivotal 1991 meeting with Donald Judd, when his compositions tightened into flatter, darker, more rigorously rectangular fields.

The show closes with four works on hanji, the traditional mulberry paper Yun took up during a stay in Paris in the early 1980s and returned to seriously in the 2000s — a softer, more absorbent surface than canvas that let pigment bloom and spread on its own terms. Archival material throughout documents the Seogyo-dong house itself, letting the paintings sit alongside the domestic and biographical context — Yun's imprisonment after protesting a school scandal in 1973, the death of his father-in-law and early mentor Kim Whanki in 1974 — that shaped the work's austerity.

Yun died in 2007, but his reputation has only grown since: a 2018 retrospective at the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Korea, traveled to Venice's Palazzo Fortuny, and his paintings sit in the permanent collections of Tate Modern and the Art Institute of Chicago among others. This is a rare chance to see three decades of his development in one place, presented by the gallery that has represented his estate for years.

shows.title: The Nearest Faraway Place
shows.description:
Friedrich Kunath paints the ache of being somewhere while wishing you were somewhere else, and his first Seoul solo show gives that feeling two full floors to unfold. Downstairs, watercolor drawings work through half-formed ideas — a candy-colored Porsche sinking into a still pond is a typical Kunath gag-turned-elegy, funny and a little heartbroken at once. Upstairs, larger oil paintings open into wide, cinematic landscapes lit by the gallery's skylight, where his recurring lone figures stare down sunsets that always seem to be receding.

Kunath, who splits his time between Los Angeles and Europe, works a vein of West Coast melancholy shot through with German Romantic longing — he's said he wants his paintings to feel like songs, and there's a similar economy of gesture here: a silhouette, a horizon, a punchline that turns wistful on a second look. The show pulls from his full toolkit of vernacular references — pop lyrics, road-trip iconography, sunset kitsch — without ever losing the sense that all this outward-looking imagery is really about the difficulty of feeling at home in yourself.

It's a good introduction to an artist who's easy to underestimate on first glance; the humor is real, but so is the sadness underneath it, and seeing the drawings and paintings together across two floors makes the throughline between the two registers clearer than any single canvas could.
shows.reception: Frieze Week Neighborhood Nights, Sep 1, 2026, 11am - 9pm (extended hours)

shows.title: Irreparable Repairs
shows.description:
Kader Attia has spent two decades treating "repair" as both a physical act and a philosophical lens for looking at colonial history and collective trauma, and his first Seoul solo show is a concentrated dose of that thinking. The centerpiece works are canvases from his long-running Mirrors series: Attia slices into the fabric, then hand-stitches the cuts back together, leaving visible scars rather than smoothing them away. The point isn't camouflage — it's that any repair announces the wound it's covering.

The show also introduces new sculptural work: everyday plastic shopping bags cast in brightly colored glass, freezing a throwaway object into permanence, and a trio of "wounded" convex mirrors in black glass, cut into so that viewers' own reflections come back distorted and interrupted. These mirror pieces draw on the eerie tradition of "witch mirrors" in old Flemish portraiture, but Attia reframes that distortion as a comment on algorithmic life today — a mirror that no longer shows you cleanly, if it ever did.

Attia is Algerian-French and has built his career on making colonial and personal history physically legible in his materials rather than just referencing it conceptually, and this show arrives while he's also showing in the Venice Biennale and preparing to curate the 2027 Kochi Biennale — useful context for a Seoul audience meeting this body of work for the first time. It rewards slow looking: the stitching, the cuts, the glass all ask you to notice the labor of mending rather than its result.

shows.title: Per Mano
shows.description:
Georg Baselitz died in April 2026, and Per Mano — planned with the artist before his death — plays as both homage and epitaph. It brings together two monotype series from the final decade of his career: the Schatten (Shadow) paintings and the Darkness Goldness works, neither previously shown in Korea. Both series find the ninety-something Baselitz still wringing new implications out of the upside-down figuration that defined his whole practice since the late 1960s.

The Schatten works take their cue from the curved shadow in Titian's portrait of Archbishop Filippo Archinto, which Baselitz rehearses, inverted, in loose, urgent strokes; look closely and inverted skulls surface within the gestural mass, a vanitas motif that runs all the way back to his 1960s Pandämonium paintings. The technique itself is physical and unrepeatable — canvas painted flat on the floor, then transferred by pressing and dragging a broom over a second canvas, so each monotype comes out singular. The Darkness Goldness paintings turn to a different register: enormous gilded hands emerging from black grounds, an aging artist's meditation on his own hand rendered with a flickering, almost ghostly presence.

Seen together, the two series make an unusually direct late-career statement about mortality from an artist not known for sentimentality — gestures that are still combative and physical, applied to a subject (his own bodily decline, his own legacy) he'd mostly circled rather than confronted head-on. For Ropac's Seoul program, which has built a strong relationship with Baselitz over the years, this is as close to a memorial exhibition as a commercial gallery gets.

shows.title: Little Things, Delightful Greetings (소소, 반색)
shows.description:
Kang Yo-Bae's first Hakgojae show in four years turns his attention from the grand and historical to the small and passing-by. Kang made his name as a central figure of Korea's Minjung art movement, painting the ruptures of modern Korean history — most famously the Jeju April 3rd massacre — with a documentary directness that gave landscape painting real political weight. This exhibition keeps his deep attachment to Jeju Island's nature and seasons intact but redirects the same searching eye toward single trees, fallen fruit, a passing cat: things ordinarily too minor to register.

The paintings, mostly acrylic on canvas from the past few years, don't abandon the sense of accumulated time that defines Kang's landscapes — he has always treated a view not as a fixed scene but as a layering of seasons and memory lived on the same patch of ground. What's different here is scale of attention rather than substance: the show reads as a natural extension of a decades-long practice rather than a break from it, the same conviction that nature and human life share one order, now trained on the overlooked rather than the monumental.

For anyone who knows Kang mainly through his history paintings, this is a chance to see the quieter, observational side of an artist whose reputation was built on confronting Korea's twentieth-century traumas — and a reminder that the two modes have always come from the same place.

shows.title: Solo Solo Solo (개인전개인전개인전)
shows.description:
Three painters share Hakgojae's new building, but the gallery has deliberately refused to unify them into a conventional group show — instead of a shared theme, visitors get three self-contained solo presentations installed in parallel, an experiment in what happens when curatorial connective tissue is withheld. It's a pointed response to the usual logic of group exhibitions, which tend to smooth over differences between artists in service of a tidy narrative.

GOODMORNINGTOWN builds unexpected friction between images, cutting across pictorial logic to generate odd, glitchy juxtapositions on canvas. SOON Yiji works in a register that mixes humor with unease, populating small-scale paintings and watercolors with deadpan, diaristic titles and a loose, sketchbook-like intimacy — her section of the show is by far the largest, filling the space with dozens of modestly-sized works. JOO Jaebum returns to the pixel as a basic unit of image-making, using sprayed acrylic on wood and resin to reverse-engineer how digital images cohere and get read, in sculptural reliefs and panels that behave more like objects than paintings.

Walking between the three distinct rooms of work, the connections that do emerge — a shared interest in fragmentation, in the small unit versus the whole — feel found rather than imposed, which is really the point of the exercise.

shows.title: Mr.: On the Threshold of Tomorrow
shows.description:
Mr., the Japanese neo-pop painter and longtime collaborator of Takashi Murakami's Kaikai Kiki studio, returns to Perrotin Seoul for his first show at the gallery's Dosan Park space and his first Seoul solo in nearly a decade. The exhibition follows a major museum survey at the Fukuoka Asian Art Museum earlier in 2026 and pushes further into the same territory: paintings, works on paper and a large sculpture built from the visual vocabulary of manga, anime and otaku culture.

Mr.'s pictures layer eras rather than choosing between them — vintage signage and nostalgic snack packaging sit next to distinctly contemporary teenage girls with dip-dyed hair, smartphones and bubble tea, so that a single canvas can feel like it's showing 1980s Japan and right-now Seoul at once. A new large-scale sculpture extends one of his recurring characters into three dimensions, letting viewers walk around a figure normally locked into a single painted viewpoint, while several shaped canvases break out of the rectangular frame entirely.

Underneath the candy-colored surfaces is a more personal undertow: Mr. has spoken about drawing and anime as a refuge from a difficult childhood, and his obsessive accumulation of everyday ephemera reads, on reflection, as a way of processing memory rather than simply celebrating pop culture. It's a dense, maximalist show, and a good one for anyone curious how the Superflat generation's imagery has aged into something more layered and elegiac.

shows.title: Undefined Panorama
shows.description:
Yang Ah Ham's first solo show at Art Sonje Center in sixteen years pulls together the many threads of Undefined Panorama, a research project she has been building since 2018 out of an older, still longer engagement with how social systems shape individual lives. The centerpiece is a new eight-channel video installation, Undefined Panorama 4.0, built as a large circular structure that viewers walk into rather than simply watch — a physical staging of the project's recurring idea that endings loop back into beginnings.

The project began after a 2014 disaster in Korea forced Ham to confront what an artist's response to systemic collapse and collective grief could look like. Since then she has tracked the machinery of neoliberalism, financialization, digital capitalism and the climate crisis, and how those large forces register in ordinary bodies and daily routines. Alongside the new video work, the show includes a companion piece, Listening Speaker, Speaking Other, which gathers private monologues collected online and threads them into the larger social narrative, plus earlier works from the Undefined Panorama lineage and related archival material spanning back to 2015.

Ham, who trained in painting and art theory in Seoul before studying media art at NYU, has spent decades examining how individuals and communities absorb the systems around them, showing at venues from the Gwangju Biennale to transmediale Berlin and the Taipei Fine Arts Museum. This exhibition functions as a career-spanning look at one sustained inquiry — less a retrospective than a chance to see how a single body of thought has grown and mutated across eight years of work.

shows.title: Pig
shows.description:
Muyeong Kim's first museum solo show takes over the Art Hall in Art Sonje Center's basement, a real theater rather than a white cube, and treats it as the actual subject of the work rather than just a venue. Kim has spent his practice picking apart the mechanics of theatrical illusion — stages, sightlines, backstage rigging — and here he gets to work inside an actual proscenium that is itself slated for renovation, giving the whole show an undertone of a space caught between disappearance and use.

The exhibition combines new photographs shot on Sorok Island (long associated with Korea's forced isolation of Hansen's disease patients) with a black-and-white series made inside Seodaemun Prison History Hall during its own renovation, plus new sculptural work. The black-and-white photographs revisit early hand-coloring photographic techniques — processes invented to fake the color of reality — recast through a contemporary lens, echoing the show's interest in artifice and apparatus.

The title refers to "pig iron" counterweights that hang unseen backstage to balance stage machinery: essential, invisible infrastructure that makes the illusion of a performance possible. That's the show's real subject — the hidden material and historical scaffolding behind spectacle. Kim, born in 1995 and winner of the first Amado Art Prize in 2024, has shown at No.9 Cork Street in London and Amado Art Space in Seoul; this show marks his most ambitious staging yet of that inquiry into theater as physical structure.

shows.title: Who Lived Happily Ever After?
shows.description:
Simon Fujiwara brings his recurring alter-ego Who the Bær to Seoul for the first time, casting the shape-shifting cartoon bear as the hero of a suite of new paintings built around myths and fairytales. Who has appeared over the past several years as a kind of empty vessel for identity — a cute, marketable form that Fujiwara pours different cultural anxieties into — and here he is refracted through the archetypes of folklore: witches, castles, transformation scenes, the moral machinery of bedtime stories. The paintings are hung in a sequence of rooms each painted a different color, turning the gallery itself into a set of themed chambers you pass through, more storybook than white cube.

Fujiwara has always worked at the seam between autobiography, branding and myth, and Who the Bær is his cleverest device yet for doing it: a character cute enough to be merchandised and blank enough to hold whatever narrative gets projected onto it. Putting Who inside "happily ever after" is a way of asking what that phrase actually promises, and to whom — the show plays the sweetness of fairytale imagery against the more unsettled question of whether an identity built for public consumption can ever really settle into an ending.

This is Fujiwara's fourth exhibition with Esther Schipper and the first at the gallery's Seoul location, opened alongside Frieze Seoul week. For viewers who know his video and installation work, this is a chance to see him working purely in paint, using the built-in familiarity of cartoon language to smuggle in stranger material.

shows.title: GRACE
shows.description:
GRACE marks the reopening of Gallery Baton in its expanded Hannam-dong space, and it does so with a survey-style hang across two floors that reads like a condensed history of the gallery's own program. The late Chun Kook-kwang's welded-pipe sculpture and Huh Dal Jae's red-ink, gold-powder landscape sit alongside Liam Gillick's powder-coated aluminum wall relief and a large Jonathan Monk canvas that literally borrows a wall text from Gillick as its subject — a small joke about authorship that sets the tone for the whole hang.

Painting carries most of the show: Rosa Loy's casein-on-canvas figures, Andi Fischer's loose oil-stick scenes, Bin Woo Hyuk's riverside canvas, Rinus Van de Velde's charcoal drawing, and newer canvases from Bae Yoon Hwan, Minyoung Choi, Christian Hidaka and Suzanne Song trace very different routes back to the same medium. Tatsuo Miyajima's LED counter piece and Noémie Goudal's underwater film provide the show's two departures into light and time-based work, while embroidered and beaded pieces by Choi Soo Jung and Koh San Keum add a textile counterpoint to all the paint.

There's no single curatorial thesis beyond "here is what this gallery does," and that's really the point — GRACE is a reintroduction, a chance to see two decades of represented artists, Korean and international, painters and sculptors, side by side in a brand-new building. It's a good entry point for anyone unfamiliar with the program and a satisfying refresher for anyone who already knows it.

shows.title: Idyll by the Tide
shows.description:
Mike Lee returns to Jason Haam for his second solo show with the gallery, following 2023's Homecoming, with a set of paintings that trade his earlier interiors for open, coastal light. Titles like The Hidden Cove Bathed in Noon Light, Overlooking the Western Sea and Low Tide point to a sustained look at shorelines — dunes, rock pools, headlands and picnic scenes rendered with the loose, sunbaked palette of a Korean summer.

Lee has built his reputation on anonymous figures whose emotional weight comes through gesture and atmosphere rather than narrative detail, and that approach carries over here even as the setting shifts outdoors: seated women in striped bodices and yellow dresses appear folded into the landscapes, still lifes of fruit and broccoli are staged against cliffs, and the sea itself becomes as much a subject as the people in front of it.

Idyll by the Tide reads as a warmer, more expansive chapter in Lee's ongoing project — less about a single moment of feeling, as his earlier work often was, and more about the slower accumulation of a season by the water. It's a good entry point for newcomers to his work and a clear step forward for those who know Homecoming.

shows.title: The Lost Garden of Heaven
shows.description:
Andrea Galvani's first solo show in Korea turns Tang Contemporary's Seoul space into a strange indoor orchard. Fourteen ceramic "botanical towers" reproduce, apple by hand-modeled apple, dozens of heirloom and extinct varieties that Galvani reconstructed from historical agricultural records with the help of farmers, pomologists and horticulturalists — a sculptural inventory of cultivars the world has quietly let disappear. The mirror-polished steel bases and stacked porcelain fruit make the towers feel both botanical and monumental, like specimen cases scaled up into architecture.

Two other bodies of work extend the show's meditation on lost time. The video sculpture "The Void Migrates to the Surface [Blue Morpho]" uses ultra-high-speed slow-motion capture to stretch the fleeting life of a Blue Morpho butterfly toward the span of an average human life, while the sound piece "Resurrection I" plays reconstructed calls of seven bird species that went extinct across the twentieth century. A neon wall sculpture, "Study on Omega-Minus," charts a landmark mid-century particle physics discovery in luminous line — Galvani's way of tying the show's ecological grief to a broader, stranger cosmology of matter and time.

Galvani, an Italian-born conceptual artist based between New York and Mexico City, works across photography, video, sound and installation with a research-driven, almost scientific method; this project alone drew on three years of collaboration with institutions including the North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences and Cornell's bioacoustics center. The result isn't a simple elegy — it's an immersive, color-saturated environment that asks visitors to sit with extinction, revival and deep time all at once, closer to a natural history diorama reimagined by an artist than a conventional gallery show.

shows.title: The Plural
shows.description:
Yeoreum Jeong, winner of the 15th DOOSAN Yonkang Arts Award, builds this show around a newly commissioned video that follows the true story of a Korean man who left home in the 1920s to search for his father and ended up drifting through Vietnam and across the Trans-Siberian Railway, swept along by the political currents of the East Asian Cold War rather than steering by his own convictions. Jeong intercuts documentary footage of present-day locations with archival material and a narrating voice that singles out the moments where his private choices collided with history, and as the film pulls back, the individual dissolves into "the plural" — the anonymous masses who lived through the same events without ever being named.

Two text-based installations extend the argument to people left out of that frame entirely. The Shepherd follows a woman riding the Trans-Siberian Railway with no destination, holding onto the smell she inherited from her mother as her only proof of self; Apron of the Low Place gives voice to a servant whose devotion to a master who owns nothing quietly costs her everything. Both works, presented as books and looping soundtracks, sit alongside the main video to ask where power actually originates and who gets to hold it.

Jeong has spent recent years digging into the layered histories of specific places — comparing archival records against present-day landscapes to surface forgotten or discordant memories — and this show, curated by Jinyoung You, is her most ambitious treatment of that method yet, tracing lives that official history flattens into statistics. It's a dense, research-heavy exhibition, but a rewarding one for anyone interested in how personal biography gets swallowed by geopolitics.

shows.title: Double Skin
shows.description:
Suyeon Kim's paintings read at first like straightforward figure studies — lovers, dancers, seated women rendered in mixed media on canvas — until the titles start doing their own strange work. Each piece in Double Skin carries a string of numbers alongside its name (a temperature, a percentage, another decimal), a private notation system that turns the paintings into records of something more like a felt condition than a described scene.

The show's title gestures at that doubling: a skin as the visible surface of a body, and a second, invisible skin made of sensation, memory or circumstance that the numbers seem to be tracking. Works like The Lovers, The Choice and The Journey sit alongside a series of large graphite-and-crayon studies of dancers in motion, suggesting a practice that moves fluidly between finished, worked-over paintings and looser, more immediate drawing.

Kim has shown steadily at GALLERY2's Seoul space, and this exhibition finds her figures more ambiguous and interior than descriptive — bodies caught in states (fear, wish, impasse) rather than in specific narratives. It's a compact, image-dense show, worth seeing for the tension between the polish of the paintings and the raw, diaristic quality of the numbers attached to them.

shows.title: The Epoch of Totalitarianism IV: The Slow Motion Chaos of Bread and Circuses
shows.description:
Los Angeles artist Umar Rashid has spent two decades constructing an "Alternative History" — a sprawling fictional saga of empires, conquests and colonial-era power struggles told through a painting language borrowed from illuminated manuscripts, ukiyo-e prints and Persian miniatures, populated by marginalized figures written back into the center of the story. This fourth chapter of his ongoing Epoch of Totalitarianism series shifts his usual terrain of war and conquest sideways, into tourism, leisure, sport, branding and entertainment — the softer machinery through which power and consumption actually operate day to day.

Familiar scenes of vacation and pleasure become stages where ancient deities, invented armies and pop-culture debris collide; violence recedes to the margins while advertising, spectacle and leisure move to the front. Rashid extends the fictional world beyond canvas into flags, garment-like textile works and installation pieces, treating the gallery itself as another territory to be colonized by his invented history.

Rashid has shown at MoMA PS1, LACMA and the Hammer Museum, and his flat color, bold outline and hybrid image-and-text approach make his paintings immediately legible even at a glance — though the density of historical and mythological reference rewards a much slower look. This is his first outing at Leeahn's Seoul space and a good introduction for anyone who hasn't encountered his work outside museum survey shows.

shows.title: Dream Weaver
shows.description:
Alex Dodge builds his paintings the way a programmer builds software: in layers of logic, each one dependent on the one beneath it. For his second solo show at BB&M, the American artist pushes that method toward the vocabulary of textiles, treating the "weave" as a structural idea rather than a literal subject. Grids, wefts and interlacing patterns recur across the canvases, standing in for the way code, image and material get knitted together in his process.

The paintings begin as 3D models, get filtered through custom software, and only then arrive at the studio, where Dodge cuts stencils and builds up surfaces by hand in paint. The result is a body of work that looks machine-precise from a distance and noticeably handmade up close — brushwork, masking edges and small errors sit right alongside crisp, digitally-derived geometry. That friction between the programmed and the physical is the real engine of the show.

The title nods to the woozy, half-remembered logic of dreaming as much as to weaving itself, and to the early years of digital culture when code and image first started generating self-contained worlds. Seen together, the works read less like a single statement and more like a sustained investigation — of how much of a hand-made object can be planned in advance, and how much has to be discovered by making it.

shows.title: (Un)Trustworthy Hearts
shows.description:
Vivi Zhu stages her solo show as a visit to "Pure Love Hospital," a fictional clinic that diagnoses and classifies love the way a doctor reads symptoms. Visitors move through the space guided by a clinical-sounding voiceover, and each work becomes a "case file" in an argument about how heterosexual romance norms have historically organized women's bodies, labor, and desire under patriarchal capitalism.

The five works on view range widely in material and tone: a video installation shot in an illegal massage parlor in Abu Dhabi that equates trafficked women with ornamental aquarium fish; a set of decaying, flesh-wrapped Tamagotchis that stage a Japanese kuroko stagehand reclaiming her own invisibility as pleasure rather than sacrifice; a video built around China's "one-day boyfriend" otome-game role-play culture; a tender two-channel portrait project following Zhu's grandparents, whose arranged marriage during the Cultural Revolution slowly became something like love; and a documentary-style single channel work about a Huai opera troupe refusing to abandon their condemned Shanghai theater.

Zhu, working across video, sculpture, and installation, is less interested in debunking "fake" love than in showing how care, performance, and resistance slip out of the categories institutions try to impose on them. Curated by independent curator Sun Kim as part of LOOP's annual Open Call, the show is a sharp, research-driven entry point into LOOP's new eco-feminist program in its freshly opened Euljiro space, and rewards slow viewing given how much text and video duration each "case" carries.
shows.reception: Opening Friday, August 14, 2026, 5pm; Artist Talk Friday, August 21, 2026, 5pm

shows.title: at the point
shows.description:
Son Jihyeong paints in thick, textured layers of oil and wax, building up surfaces where color behaves almost like sediment — particles that accumulate into ridges, cracks, and unexpected topographies rather than settling into a legible image. At the point, she pushes that logic further by staging her canvases alongside vintage European Bauhaus-era furniture from mk2, letting paintings and functional objects share the same room as equal, interacting presences rather than art on one side and decor on the other.

The paintings themselves stay resolutely abstract: works like pin stripe and crinkle read as fields of ridged, mottled color rather than pictures of anything, the product of Son's long habit of observing plant life and gradually deciding that color, not outline, is where form actually lives. Titles like "moist slice" and "unrolling" hint at organic processes — peeling, cutting, layering — without ever resolving into recognizable subjects.

The premise (paintings + furniture as one integrated environment) is a modest but effective curatorial idea, treating the gallery's white cube as a livable space rather than a neutral backdrop, and it fits Son's own sense of paint as a physical, near-sculptural material rather than a purely optical one.

shows.title: Chapter II 2026 Residency Exhibition
shows.artist: Park Ji Won, Byun Chae Young, Choi Mo Min
shows.description:
Chapter II closes out its 2026 studio residency with a three-artist show that reads like three separate investigations of domestic space held in the same room. Park Ji Won paints specific Seoul addresses and interiors — a Hannam-daero alley, a house's single room — turning found architecture into quietly charged psychological portraits. Byun Chae Young works in a rougher, more visceral register, with pieces titled "vestiges" that treat furniture (a bed, a restraint) as the residue of bodies that have already left the scene.

Choi Mo Min rounds out the show with a suite of paintings — "Painter's House," "A Room with a Tree," "To Wash Away," "Going Out" — that follow a single recurring interior through washing, leaving, and returning, giving the whole exhibition a loose narrative arc from room to room.

Together the three practices share a fascination with the house as a site where memory, labor, and the body leave physical traces, making this residency show a useful cross-section of what a younger generation of Korean painters is doing with the domestic interior right now. It's a compact, single-gallery show, but the range between Park's cool documentary eye, Byun's abraded surfaces, and Choi's narrative sequencing makes it worth the visit.

shows.title: KAWS: Friends and Neighbors
shows.description:
This is KAWS's first solo museum exhibition in Korea, and it leans into the idea of relationships as the real subject of his cartoon-faced figures. Brian Donnelly built his visual language on the street — graffiti and advertising interventions in 1990s New York and New Jersey — before moving it into painting, sculpture, and product design without ever fully leaving any of those registers behind. Here that whole range is on view: large new paintings, oversized bronze and painted sculptures, and the instantly recognizable X-eyed characters recast as protagonists in scenes of friendship, rivalry, and unease.

The show's premise is that "friend" and "neighbor" are two different kinds of closeness — one chosen, one accidental — and that both carry tension along with comfort. Works like "The Red Ball" put two figures in a literal tug-of-war on a playground, while standalone bronzes such as "The Long View" and "Measuring Shadows" isolate single figures on pedestals like specimens, gazing into the distance rather than at each other. A recurring multi-figure piece, "Therapy," lines up eleven of KAWS's CHUM characters holding a single canvas that only resolves into one image when seen as a group — a fairly literal, and effective, visual joke about needing other people to complete a picture.

Twenty works are on view in total, including several new pieces made for this exhibition, spread through Space K's column-free, naturally lit galleries in Magok. It's a good entry point for anyone who knows KAWS mainly from collectibles and collaborations and wants to see the sculptural and painterly side of the practice at full scale.

shows.title: Mountains as Mountains, Waters as Waters
shows.description:
Soonik Kwon has spent more than a decade building two parallel bodies of abstract work — "Absence of Ego," made from thousands of repeated dots and rubbed graphite, and "Interstice: Pile Up & Rub," which translates the cyclical push and pull of yin and yang into overlapping planes of color derived from dancheong, the traditional palette used on Korean temple architecture. This show, centered on both series, catches him at a hinge point: alongside the accumulation-based paintings he's known for, he's begun experimenting with gwiyal, a broad, loaded-brush technique that trades the earlier work's dense, meditative buildup for something more open and gestural.

The title borrows a line of Zen non-explanation — a mountain is simply a mountain — that fits Kwon's own description of these as "paintings that need no explanation." Nothing here is a symbol standing in for something else; the graphite-rubbed surfaces and interlocking color fields are meant to be encountered as physical facts, built through countless small, repeated gestures rather than a single decisive image. It's slow, exacting work that asks for the same patience from a viewer that the artist brought to making it — closer looking reveals the grain of the hand's movement, the accumulated time embedded in the surface.

For a gallery that mostly shows Japanese and Chinese postwar and contemporary art, this solo outing is a chance to see a significant Korean abstractionist's four-decade evolution from figuration to a highly controlled, materially rich abstraction, timed to coincide with the release of his illustrated essay collection.
shows.reception: Saturday, August 29, 2026, 3-6pm (opening reception with book launch of Kwon's illustrated essay, From the Interstice to Light)

shows.title: Míope
shows.description:
Marina Rheingantz's first solo exhibition in Korea gathers a suite of new landscape paintings that never quite resolve into a fixed view. The show takes its title from the Portuguese word for "nearsighted," and that condition of blurred, shifting focus runs through everything on view: fields of mauve, ochre and lavender that read as botanical one moment and pure abstraction the next, painted with a pointillist precision that sits oddly against passages of enveloping haze. The largest canvas, "Pipa," floats a cloud-like form over a pink expanse that could be sky or scrubland, refusing to let the eye settle on foreground or horizon.

Rheingantz builds her paintings through repeated layering and stripping away — turpentine-thinned pigment bleeding down the canvas, forms surfacing and receding like sediment. Smaller works such as "Periquita," "Caracol" and "Taturana" take on the look of weathered plaster or peeling wallpaper, while an embroidered piece, "Outono," made in collaboration with the artist's mother and a Uruguayan textile artisan, extends her interest in pattern into actual thread and stitch. Titles throughout point to plants and creatures native to Brazil, anchoring otherwise ungrounded compositions to the artist's memories of growing up in rural Araraquara.

Rheingantz, who lives and works in São Paulo, has had recent solo shows at ICA Milano, Bortolami in New York and the Musée des Beaux-Arts in Nîmes, and her work sits in collections including Tate and the Centre Pompidou. What makes this body of work distinct is its explicit departure from Western linear perspective in favor of a more relational, East Asian-inflected sense of space — pictures built from shifting intervals rather than a single vantage point, which gives the whole show a quietly disorienting, atmospheric charge.

shows.title: Claire's Camera
shows.artist: Nicolas Bermeo, Bailey Connolly, Isaiah Davis, Audrey Gair, Jiyoon Chung, Sangwoo Kim, Nandi Loaf, Isabelle Frances McGuire, Sveta Mordovskaya, Sunwoo, Kira Scerbin, Joe Speier, Michelle Uckotter, Elis & Parker von Sternberg
shows.description:
Named for Hong Sang-soo's 2017 film about chance encounters and secondhand observation at the Cannes Film Festival, this group show is a collaboration between N/A and the New York gallery King's Leap, bringing fourteen artists from both galleries' rosters into the same rooms. It opened as the anchor event of Euljiro Night, the Seoul Art Week neighborhood evening that kicks off Frieze Seoul's citywide programming, and runs deep into October.

With this many artists across such a compressed Euljiro space, the show reads less like a thesis exhibition than a series of conversations — paintings, sculpture, and object-based work rubbing against each other the way strangers do in a Hong Sang-soo film, each piece a fragment of observation rather than part of a single unified argument. It's the kind of survey where the pleasure is in the juxtapositions: N/A regulars like Jiyoon Chung and Sunwoo showing alongside King's Leap's New York-based artists, none of whom have had much exposure in Seoul before.

For visitors unfamiliar with either gallery's program, this is an efficient way to get a read on the sensibility N/A has built its reputation on since opening in this former hardware-store space — a gallery unafraid of loose, essayistic group shows over tidy curatorial statements — while also getting a preview of what King's Leap's younger New York artists are doing right now.
shows.reception: Monday, August 31, 2026 (Euljiro Night, Seoul Art Week)

shows.title: Becoming With
shows.artist: Joohyun Kim, MeeNa Park, Yo-E Ryou
shows.description:
This three-artist show takes relation itself as its subject: each of the three participants approaches connection from a completely different angle, and the gallery lets their independent bodies of work sit side by side rather than forcing a shared thesis. Yo-E Ryou draws on her research into breath, the body and water — an interest that runs through her work with Jeju's haenyeo free-diving communities — turning physical sensation into image and object. Joohyun Kim works from a background in topology, building compositions that expand outward through repeated, rule-based structures until they resolve into light and pattern rather than illustration.

MeeNa Park's contribution turns on a more everyday kind of relation: the gap between the name of a color and its physical reality, and the misunderstandings that gap produces. Her work treats color as a manufactured, networked object rather than an abstract idea, which gives the show's more cerebral through-line — how meaning gets made between people, materials and systems — a very tactile counterpoint.

Seen together, the three practices don't illustrate a single argument so much as demonstrate one: that individual work only becomes legible in relation to something else, whether that's a body of water, a mathematical structure, or a swatch of paint chips. It's a quiet, well-paired group show rather than a spectacle, worth a visit for anyone interested in how Korean artists working in very different registers can be put into productive conversation.

shows.title: Ostranenie
shows.artist: Jina Park, Julius Hofmann, Lucas Kaiser, Tilo Baumgärtel
shows.description:
Ostranenie borrows its title from the Russian Formalist idea of "defamiliarization" — the technique of making the ordinary strange again so it can actually be seen — and uses it to frame four painters who each bend familiar imagery slightly out of true. Jina Park's egg-and-oil-tempera panels, including a multi-part Cabinet of Birds, use an old-master technique to paint subjects that sit somewhere between naturalist illustration and unsettling allegory. Tilo Baumgärtel's canvases and lithographs stage groups of figures in flatly lit, faintly absurd tableaux that read like folk tales missing their moral.

Julius Hofmann's acrylics turn souvenir-postcard imagery — a shell, a Berlin cityscape, a swamp scene — into slightly too-bright, too-flat compositions that feel like memories replayed at the wrong saturation. Lucas Kaiser's oil landscapes, all harvested fields and overcast skies, are the most traditionally "painterly" works here, but placed against the others they start to look staged too, like backdrops rather than views.

None of these four is Korean, and the show's real interest is in watching different national painting traditions — German, and otherwise European figurative and landscape painting — run through a shared curatorial idea of strangeness-through-familiarity. It's a tightly hung, unshowy group exhibition, but the pairing of Park's tempera technique against the others' acrylic and oil surfaces makes for good contrasts in how each artist manufactures unease.

shows.title: White Noise
shows.description:
White Noise pairs the godfather of video art with a much younger artist working in AI-driven imagery, treating both as thinkers about what happens when humans live alongside a new kind of machine. On the Paik side, a cello-shaped television sculpture recalls his performances with cellist Charlotte Moorman, shown together with nude drawings and monitor works whose footage once played on the screens of that same TV Cello — plus a nod to TV Buddha, Paik's own uneasy meditation on a medium he otherwise championed. It's a chance to see Paik's analog-electronic vocabulary in a gallery setting rather than a museum retrospective.

Kim Ryu answers with newer, stranger machines. Deus Ex Machina is a sculpture whose sensor-driven eye appears to track viewers around the room, though the movement is actually a fixed pattern rather than real recognition — a small deception aimed at how readily we assume AI is paying attention to us. Anonymous Montage_13 Clues and the Agents' Outputs goes further, fusing painting, sculpture, AI-generated imagery and 3D-printed elements into one work that keeps drifting out of sync with itself, fed by webcams that generate shifting, distorted images of whoever is standing in front of it.

The show's title borrows from John Cage's 4'33", using "white noise" as a way of describing background technology that has quietly stopped feeling exceptional. Paik saw the electronic image as a new partner for humanity; Kim Ryu is more interested in what we're willing to believe about a machine that only appears to look back. Putting them in the same rooms turns a fifty-year gap in Korean media art into a single, pointed conversation about trust, attention and the tools we've decided to live with.

venue.name: Gallery Bhak (BHAK)
hours: Closed Sun, Mon and national holidays

shows.title: The Art of Loving
shows.artist: An Chorong, Noh Songhee, Lee Kangseung
shows.description:
Taking its title from Erich Fromm's 1956 treatise, this group show treats love not as a feeling that happens to you but as a discipline — something collected, practiced, and maintained through relation to other people. Curator Kim Seongwoo brings together three artists whose work is built out of other people's material: photographs someone else took, traces of other people's labor, objects and language borrowed and reassembled.

An Chorong works as a kind of relay station for images, receiving photographs taken by others, recontextualizing them, and redistributing them rather than authoring pictures from scratch — a practice that treats the photographic image itself as a site of exchange rather than possession. Noh Songhee tracks the residue of everyday labor, turning found and gathered traces into a kind of negative cartography of larger economic systems most of us only feel the edges of. Lee Kangseung collects and repurposes language, objects, and images to braid together past, present, and future into a shared queer desire that resists a single, linear narrative.

Together the three practices sketch out an idea of love that has nothing to do with ownership or the satisfaction of one's own wants, and everything to do with how a self is built from what — and who — passes through it. It's a quiet, cerebral show, more interested in method than spectacle, and rewards visitors willing to sit with photographs and objects that only reveal their logic slowly.

shows.title: All that will remain, something that will never disappear
shows.description:
Jazoo Yang's first solo show with PIBI Gallery gathers three interlocking bodies of work built from scavenged, tactile materials: a new series called Bulgasari, made with castor aralia thorns and pearl-headed pins pressed into the canvas surface, the large-scale sound-and-painting works of Skin of Everything, and a related series in which thorns are driven into the interiors of found boxes and objects. The title figure, Bulgasari, is a shape-shifting, fire-and-metal-eating creature from Korean folklore that cannot be killed — Yang uses it here as a stand-in for survival through constant transformation, a theme she has been circling since relocating between Berlin and rural Yeongdeok, where she became interested in folk ways of reading weather and land that fall outside scientific rationality.

What comes through in the images is less illustration than surface incident: canvases built up from opposing textures — thorns that grow outward to protect, pins that pierce inward — creating skin-like fields that read at once as scarred, scaled, and alive. The Skin of Everything works pair this tactile handling with sound recordings of the artist's own scraping and pressing motions, an attempt to register in audio the vibration of bodily contact with the canvas that a purely visual work can't capture.

Yang trained originally in Korean ancient history rather than art school, and came to painting self-taught in her thirties after years working in street art and urban mural projects during Korea's redevelopment boom of the 2000s — experience that shaped her long-running interest in objects, buildings, and neighborhoods that vanish without a trace. That biography is legible in the work's roughness: nothing here is smoothed over for easy viewing, and the show rewards close, slow looking at the accumulated marks of the artist's hand.

shows.title: IN SCALE
shows.artist: Lee Jae-hyung, Jung Jung-ju, Park Geun-ho, Han Seung-gu
shows.description:
IN SCALE brings together four sculptors and installation artists whose work moves fluidly between the miniature and the monumental — from hand-scale modules and maquettes up to public-scale commissions. The show's organizing idea is that "scale" covers more than physical size: it also describes how each artist's working method translates between registers, from studio object to architectural intervention to urban site.

Central to that translation is the module — not simply a repeated part, but a governing unit that lets a single formal language stay recognizable whether it's shown as a tabletop object or blown up to public-sculpture size. Expect to see the same underlying vocabulary of forms recur across drastically different scales and materials as the four artists' practices are set in dialogue with one another.

Keumsan Gallery, a longtime Jung-gu presence near Namsan, gives the show room to lay out that range across its galleries, making this a useful primer on how contemporary Korean sculptors think about the jump from private studio experiment to public artwork.

shows.title: Up Against the Walls!
shows.description:
Up Against the Walls! is a curated group exhibition at The Page Gallery organized by Seungduk Kim and Franck Gautherot, the co-directors of Le Consortium in Dijon, France — one of the longer-running and more internationally connected contemporary art centers in Europe. The exhibition's title points to a preoccupation with the wall itself: not simply as the neutral support a painting hangs on, but as a surface with its own history, texture and charge, something works can react against, cling to, or push off from.

Given the curators' track record — decades spent putting Korean and international artists into dialogue through exhibitions that treat abstraction, painting and object-making as part of one continuous conversation — expect a show built around juxtaposition rather than a single medium or generation. Kim and Gautherot have a longstanding interest in Korean modernist and monochrome painting alongside Western minimal and post-minimal art, and their past collaborations with The Page Gallery and with institutions like Gwangju's Asia Culture Center suggest this outing will again mix eras and geographies rather than present a tidy survey of one scene.

For Seoul audiences, the appeal is less about seeing a single artist's full arc and more about watching two veteran European curators reframe how paintings and wall-based works can be read against each other in a Korean gallery context — a chance to see how ideas travel between Dijon and Seoul. Anyone interested in how curatorial pairing itself becomes a kind of authorship should find this a rewarding, if less predictable, late-summer show.

shows.title: Eun-Me Ahn's Sculpture Show
shows.description:
Eun-Me Ahn has spent most of her career on stage, as one of Korea's most recognizable contemporary choreographers, known for riotous color, cropped hair and a body language that refuses stillness. This show, staged across museumhead's ground floor and outdoor area in Gyedong, moves that same restless physicality into three-dimensional objects — her first outing as a sculptor rather than a dance-maker.

Structures were designed with architect Donghee Kim and fabricated by Soomin Park, giving the works a built, load-bearing presence that plays against Ahn's usual medium of the moving body; where dance disappears the moment it happens, these pieces stay put, letting a viewer walk around and return to them. The graphic design and accompanying texts (by Geun-jun and Chungwoo-Michael Lim) frame the show as a continuation of Ahn's long interest in the body as spectacle, just recast in a material that doesn't need a stage.

For a small project space known for backing younger, experimental artists, hosting a major performing artist's first sculptural exhibition is a notable swerve — worth a visit for anyone curious what happens when a choreographer's sense of motion gets frozen into form.

shows.title: Rigorous Hands
shows.artist: Jinsik Yoo, Sungoo Im, Sooji Lee, Sanoh Lee, Donghoon Rhee, Leebinsoyeon, Miyeon Yi, Yoo Jung Ellie Choi
shows.description:
Rigorous Hands gathers eight artists from drawingRoom's roster around a simple but demanding premise: that the physical labor of making — the hours of sewing, wood carving, papier-mâché building, and hand-thrown ceramics — is itself a form of thinking. Painting, sculpture, and installation share the room, but the works are unified less by medium than by process: material choices like wood, paper, graphite, thread, and clay each carry their own resistance and logic, and the artists let that resistance shape the final form.

What comes through across the group is a shared interest in how repetitive, bodily work organizes memory and personal history. Jinsik Yoo's ceramics, trained partly in Simone Leigh's studio, carry a sculptural weight that belies their material's fragility. Sanoh Lee and Sungoo Im, both working across ceramic and painterly languages, use accumulation and craft process to excavate personal and cultural narratives, while Donghoon Rhee, Leebinsoyeon, Miyeon Yi, Sooji Lee, and Yoo Jung Ellie Choi each bring distinct approaches — from textile-based figuration to information design translated into physical form — to the same question of what slow, exacting handwork can reveal about everyday experience.

The show is drawingRoom's presentation for Frieze Seoul season, timed to align with the citywide fair calendar, and it functions as a useful survey of a gallery program built around emerging and mid-career Korean artists working in labor-intensive, materially specific ways.

shows.title: Once Upon Now
shows.description:
Chris Ro trained as an architect and works as a graphic designer, and Once Upon Now feels like both backgrounds converging on a single problem: how do you hold onto a place after it's gone? The exhibition takes as its literal starting point the gallery building itself, built in 1997 as a home and later an office, and now the exhibition space Ro is populating with silkscreened and hand-drawn "afterimages" of other, lost places.

The technical core of the show is Ro's use of silkscreen printing pushed toward instability rather than precision — each pass through the mesh produces not an identical copy but a shifted, misaligned variant, so his graphic language of flattened, layered forms ends up closer to painting than to reproducible design. Framed works, an installation piece, and a set of ink drawings all circle the same idea: that the specific texture of a vanished place (its light, its foot traffic, its divisions between function and disuse) can be summoned back only as fragments, never fully restored.

It's a quietly research-driven show — Ro dug into oral histories and 1990s urban development records for the building itself — but the results read as much through mood and texture as through information. For anyone interested in how designers' formal tools (grids, layouts, print registration) can be repurposed as a way of thinking about memory and loss, this is a rewarding, unusually cerebral gallery show.

shows.title: Panvital Transcendentalism (범생명적 초월주의)
shows.artist: Hoon Kwak, Jaekwon Kim, Manyoung Han, Sukju Lee, Doobin Im, Jonghae Park, Jindu Kim, Kwangho Cho, Youngjin Kim, Sunwang Qwon, Eunsook Shin, Youngwon Kim
shows.description:
Sun Gallery revives a homegrown Korean art movement that first surfaced in November 1990, when critic Im Doo-bin proposed a decisive break from two decades of Korean painting: neither the market-distanced formalism of 1970s abstraction nor the didactic materialism of 1980s Minjung art, but a way of seeing existence itself as alive rather than inert. The dozen artists gathered here — several of them founding members of the original movement, including Im himself — have spent three decades developing that premise across painting, photography, ceramic-inflected sculpture, and mixed media.

What unites the work on view is less a shared style than a shared conviction that matter is never just matter. Manyoung Han's canvases layered with objects and repeated marks, Sukju Lee's atmospheric oil paintings, Jaekwon Kim's totemic animal figures rendered in mixed media, and Youngwon Kim's bronze figures all approach the body and the natural world as charged with something beyond their physical description. Jindu Kim's cosmological acrylic paintings and Youngjin Kim's photographic prints of nomadic figures push the same idea outward, toward landscape and migration.

Coming three decades after the movement's founding exhibitions and its invitation to Zurich's Cabaret Voltaire, the show reads as both a reunion and a rereading — a chance to see whether an idea born from specifically Korean philosophical ground still has traction now, amid the technological acceleration and social fracture the original manifesto was already worried about in 1990. It's a large, uneven, generous survey rather than a tightly edited thesis show, and it rewards viewers willing to move between very different painterly languages in search of the connective thread.
shows.reception: Thursday, September 3, 2026, 6-9pm (live performance with Doobin Im, part of Samcheong Night)

shows.title: The Cycle: Incipit — The Promise of Becoming
shows.description:
Obvious, the Paris-based trio best known for selling one of the first AI-generated paintings at auction in 2018, returns to Sun Gallery for a second show built around an unusual translation: taking the behavior of autonomous AI agents inside a digital simulation and rendering it as large-scale ceramic fresco. The agents in question interact, form loose social structures, and gradually build a shared sense of the world they inhabit — the artists observe these emergent digital societies the way an anthropologist might watch a real one, then fire their observations into clay, glaze, and pigment.

The resulting objects are deliberately pitched to look like archaeology from a civilization that hasn't happened yet — physical artifacts standing in for a culture that only exists as code. The subtitle, "The Promise of Becoming," points to the show's real subject: identity and memory once the idea of a fixed, continuous self falls away, replaced by whatever traces, records, and accumulated knowledge survive an agent's disappearance.

It's a conceptually dense premise for a very physical medium, and that friction — soft, ancient-feeling ceramic surfaces standing in for something as intangible as a generative algorithm's internal logic — is the most interesting thing the show has going for it. Worth seeing for anyone curious about where AI art goes once it stops being a flat image on a wall.

shows.title: Whiffling
shows.description:
"Whiffling" is a term for wind that keeps changing direction without warning, and Cha Minyoung uses it as a fitting title for a practice built around instability of place and perception. Working across installation and video, she has spent the past two decades probing the gap between physical location and the more slippery, constructed sense of "place" that forms around it — the way a room, a screen, or a memory can all claim to be somewhere real. Earlier bodies of work leaned on the vocabulary of charades and silent film, using wordless gesture as a stand-in for the difficulty of describing where we actually are.

This solo exhibition at PYO Gallery's Seochon space extends that inquiry, likely combining sculptural installation with projected or screen-based elements that ask viewers to physically move through a space that keeps subtly contradicting itself. It's a good match for a gallery that has spent recent seasons alternating between veteran Dansaekhwa-adjacent painters and younger, conceptually driven artists — Cha represents the latter camp, and her work rewards slow looking rather than a quick walkthrough.

For anyone exploring Seochon's gallery cluster, this is a chance to see an artist whose international exposure — from Art Dubai to Hong Kong Arts Centre survey shows — hasn't been matched by frequent solo outings in Seoul itself, making this run worth planning around.

shows.title: Future Elegy For a New Life
shows.artist: Gijeong Goo, Hyunjin Park, Soeun Bae
shows.description:
Three artists build bodies that were never meant to be biological in this group show, which treats grief and mortality as design problems rather than purely emotional ones. Gijeong Goo pairs fabricated steel structures with living plants that visitors must watch grow and wilt over the run of the show, an installation that folds real-time botanical decay into a piece about the "Biocene," a speculative future where nature reclaims governance from human hands.

Hyunjin Park's contribution centers on three sculpted dog-skull figures reimagining Cerberus, the underworld's three-headed guardian, with each head dyed in the orange of touch-me-not flowers and fused with human, canine, and floral anatomy — a direct nod to Korean folk practices around mourning, waiting, and femininity. Soeun Bae, working from casts of her own body, builds silicone and resin prosthetics and fused figures that read as tender, queer, post-human companions, more intimate than clinical despite the material vocabulary of glass, metal, and 3D-printed form.

None of the three artists resolve the questions they raise about what a body is once it stops being strictly human or strictly alive; instead the show sits in that unresolved space, using sculpture, living matter, and prosthetic form to ask what care looks like on the far side of biology. It's a small gallery, but a dense one — worth slowing down for the individual pieces rather than skimming the room.

shows.title: On Paper
shows.description:
On Paper gathers seven Korean artists — Key Minjung, Doh Hyunhee, Moon Mean, Son Seungbeom, Lee Seungae, Im Sungoo and Jang Seungkeun — who all use paper less as a neutral support than as an active, changeable material. Across the show, hanji is dyed and washed out, torn and rejoined, rubbed with graphite, or hand-made from scratch and paired with unlikely partners like stainless steel and metallic tempera, so the paper's own physical history becomes part of each image.

The works range from Doh Hyunhee's repeatedly bleached and re-inked hanji panels to Im Sungoo's drawings that are cut apart and stitched back together into new, dislocated narratives, and Son Seungbeom's quiet ink studies of weeds and stones built up through slow, obsessive mark-making. Lee Seungae extends the same sensibility into rubbings, wall-based installation and stop-motion animation, while Key Minjung and Moon Mean push hanji against industrial or handmade counterpoints to see what survives the friction.

Taken together, the exhibition is less a survey of "paper art" than a meditation on process itself — on what happens when a fragile, responsive material is folded, stained, cut and reassembled, and on how those accumulated actions become legible as image. It's a good, close-looking show for anyone curious about contemporary Korean painting and drawing practices that treat the support as seriously as the mark.

shows.title: Nap
shows.description:
Nam Hwayeon's first show since receiving the newly-renamed Ilwoo Art Award turns the entire gallery floor into a stage set for sleeping: pink carpet, office furniture, dead plants, mirrors and clocks stopped at the exact mid-afternoon moment when a nap becomes irresistible. Performers occupy the space daily, lying across chairs and tables or stretched on the floor, sometimes actually asleep, sometimes simply present — an unscripted performance work in which the sleeping body itself becomes the artwork, and visitors are invited to lie down too.

Nam has spent her career tracking how time, movement and archival material intersect, and this show extends that inquiry into the most involuntary interruption of productive time there is. A 2014 project following an ant's path returns as a series of plaster reliefs, while a new video sets brisk commands like "get up now" against the slow collapse of a melting ice figure — a blunt joke about the impossibility of forcing alertness. Between the video, sculpture, a 24-hour livestream and a recurring performance producing oversized paper cranes, the show accumulates into something between an abandoned office, a waiting room, and the tail end of a party nobody wanted to end.

It's an unusually generous, low-key show for a gallery attached to a major corporate foundation — less concerned with spectacle than with getting visitors to actually slow down inside it, which given the subject matter feels entirely appropriate.

shows.title: Proxima
shows.description:
Kim Young-Hun paints the invisible hum of electromagnetic space. For nearly two decades his two signature bodies of work, Electronic Nostalgia and the newer Frequency series, have translated the idea of vibrating waves and digital noise into layered, semi-abstract fields of stained and scraped pigment. Proxima brings together roughly twenty canvases spanning both series, including several 2026 paintings shown for the first time, and traces how his rippling, pixel-like marks have moved from picturing glitchy "virtual landscapes" toward a more physical, gestural abstraction built from the sheer weight and rhythm of paint.

The show's title borrows the name of Proxima Centauri, the sun's nearest stellar neighbor yet still unreachably distant — a fitting metaphor for Kim's interest in signals that travel across vast gaps of time and space before they reach us. Paintings like the Electronic Nostalgia series read as scarred, glowing surfaces where color seems to pulse up through sanded and re-layered skins, while the newer Frequency canvases pare that noise down into single, sustained gestures that the artist links to the East Asian idea of qi, or vital energy.

Kim, a Hongik University and Chelsea College of Art graduate whose work sits in the collections of Seoul's Leeum and the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art's art bank, has spent his career treating painting as a kind of receiver for forces we can't otherwise see. Proxima is a good introduction to that project: a chance to watch one artist's private technology of mark-making evolve from jittery digital dreaming into something closer to cosmic pulse.

shows.title: Dear Collectors, Yes, You
shows.artist: Choi Seong-im, Kang Juri, Oh Yeonjin
shows.description:
Three artists represented by The Reference — Choi Seong-im, Kang Juri, and Oh Yeonjin — share the small basement-and-mezzanine space for a show that is really an argument dressed up as an exhibition: that looking closely and looking long is the actual beginning of collecting, long before any money changes hands. The gallery, itself an art bookstore and project space, uses the show to walk visitors through that idea directly, pairing works by its three represented artists with a wall text that name-checks the Paris dealer Yvon Lambert's early, unfashionable bets on artists like Sol LeWitt and On Kawara as a model for how taste gets made.

Choi Seong-im, Kang Juri (also known as JooLee Kang), and Oh Yeonjin work in different registers — from Kang's research-driven, often text- and archive-inflected practice to more materially direct approaches from her co-exhibitors — but the show deliberately avoids grouping them by medium or theme, instead letting each artist's works sit as individual objects worth stopping in front of. It's a modest, low-key premise for a group show, closer to a curated shop window than a thesis exhibition, and that's rather the point.

Worth a visit for anyone curious about the primary market end of Korean contemporary art rather than its museum-scale spectacles: this is where new collectors actually start, in a compact Seochon space that doubles as a bookshop, with prices attached and conversation encouraged.

shows.title: 3rd Poem: Es Devlin, Come Home Again
shows.description:
Es Devlin has spent three decades designing environments for other people's spectacles — opera houses, Beyoncé and U2 tours, the closing ceremony of the London Olympics — and her first solo show in Korea turns that same stagecraft on the exhibition format itself. Come Home Again is built as a sequence of encounters rather than a chronological survey: visitors walk through a corridor of inverted books with drawings projected across their spines (Infinite Library), pass into a disorienting Mirror Maze, and stand inside a room-sized screen made from hundreds of the artist's own sketchbooks, accumulated over 35 years and projected at a scale of roughly 11.6 by 3.6 meters.

The show's centerpiece, a new work made specifically for Seoul, pairs painted plywood, sound and LED elements with drawings of endangered species from both London and Seoul, inviting visitors to learn and sing their names together — Devlin's way of tying biodiversity loss to the parallel loss of language. Two participatory pieces extend the same logic: in Collective Portrait strangers sit and draw each other, building an accumulating archive of faces over the run of the show, while Collective Reading gathers books that have shaped Devlin's thinking into a room visitors can sit in and use.

What holds the whole thing together is Devlin's long-standing interest in what she calls "Temporary Society" — the community that forms, briefly, when strangers share a room. At FUTURA SEOUL that idea gets an unusual assist from the building itself: this is the first installment of the gallery's ongoing 100 Poems series to let natural daylight into the galleries, so the light installations shift with the hour and the view onto the rear garden changes the mood of the rooms across a visit. It's a rare chance to see a major international artist's practice reconceived, rather than simply shipped in, for a specific place.

shows.title: One Year – Scenes in Time
shows.description:
Organized by Opera Gallery Seoul but staged off-site at the Seoul Calligraphy Art Museum, this is a focused survey of recent paintings by the Catalan painter Xevi Solà. Solà works from found imagery — fashion photography, film stills, archival snapshots — but rather than reproducing these sources he repaints them from instinct and memory, so figures and landscapes arrive slightly blurred, unresolved, and open to the viewer's own projection.

The paintings on view lean toward landscape after a period in which Solà concentrated on the human figure, and the show is built as a loose sequence of interconnected scenes — a beach outing, a chance encounter, a parked car — that read like stills from a film whose plot stays deliberately out of reach. His brushwork is fast and visibly improvised, prioritizing mood and gesture over exact likeness, which gives even his most everyday subjects a slightly uncanny, suspended quality.

Trained in Barcelona and now based in Girona, Solà belongs to a generation of figurative painters more interested in atmosphere than narrative closure, and this exhibition — his first major outing in Korea — is a good entry point to that sensibility: paintings that feel plucked mid-sentence from someone else's memory.
