shows.title: World Affair
shows.description:
COMPANY — the Helsinki design studio run by Korean-born Aamu Song and Finnish designer Johan Olin — has spent two decades tracking down small-scale manufacturing traditions around the world, from woodworkers in Finland's forests to market stalls in Pakistan, and this show is essentially a travelogue of that fieldwork. Rather than polished museum objects, it presents the messy, generative middle of the process: drawings made on site, conversations with makers, prototypes, and the finished goods that eventually get sold through the duo's secretive pop-up shop, Salakauppa.

Spread across four floors of Piknic's exhibition halls, the installation follows a single object's path from an artisan's hands to a market stall to someone's daily life and back again into a new idea — what the studio calls a "circulation" of respect between designer and maker. Expect natural materials worked with old techniques: wood, clay, metal, and textile, treated less as raw material for design objects than as vessels for the spiritual and technical knowledge of the communities that produced them.

COMPANY's secret-shop projects have shown at Kiasma, the Design Museum Helsinki, and Aomori Museum of Art, and the studio has collaborated with Artek, Marimekko, and Hermès, but this is a rare chance to see the research and process side of their practice laid out in full rather than the finished commercial objects alone. It's a gentle, materially rich show, well suited to Piknic's mix of gallery, café, and rooftop garden, and one of the last chances to catch it before it closes.

shows.title: Time of Photo 1: Digital, Vintage, AI
shows.description:
Kang Hong-goo has been making digital photographs since 1992, when he built his own PC from parts bought at Yongsan Electronics Market, and this survey traces that three-decade run through three distinct technical moments: early digital manipulation, the accidental "vintage-ing" of old digital prints, and his newest experiments with generative AI. It's less a greatest-hits show than an argument about what photography's supposed neutrality and reproducibility actually mean once the underlying technology keeps changing under it.

The most poignant material here is Kang's 1990s output, printed on laser printers and pieced together by hand, or transferred to slide film and enlarged — crude by today's standards, and now degrading in ways that make each print a one-of-a-kind object, an accidental "vintage print" produced by a supposedly infinitely reproducible medium. Alongside these are newer works that use Photoshop's generative AI tools to splice museum-grade ceramics into ordinary contemporary scenes, testing what happens when a priceless antique object is casually reinserted into daily life.

Kang, who has long described himself as a "B-grade artist" more interested in blunt, legible ideas than technical polish, uses the AI-generated pieces to needle at what he sees as the flattened, cliché-driven images that generative tools tend to produce — arguing that human artists retain something AI can't touch: a body that ages, tires and eventually dies, and therefore actually experiences what it depicts. It's a sharp, well-timed show for a moment when nearly every gallery has an opinion about AI imagery, argued here through the lens of someone who has watched his own tools become obsolete more than once.

shows.title: Cloud 9
shows.description:
Seong Ryul paints the kind of summer afternoon that only looks ordinary in hindsight: blinding cumulus clouds, sun-bleached playgrounds, cats dozing in alleyways, the particular blue of a sky that seems to hold still and drift at the same time. He builds these scenes in thin, translucent layers of acrylic gouache, letting water spread the pigment into soft, unforced boundaries rather than painting over the blooms and tide-lines that appear as it dries — the technique itself becomes a way of picturing time passing rather than a single frozen moment.

Trained as an animator at the Korea National University of Arts before turning to painting, Seong Ryul carries a storyteller's instinct for staging a scene, but Cloud 9 isn't really about narrative incident. It's closer to what the Busan Museum of Art's Cheong Jong Hyo has called a body of work about growth: summer here stands in for a state of maximum aliveness, clouds for time moving on, light for the way memory gets triggered by something as small as a particular quality of afternoon sun.

The show gathers recent paintings that consolidate a visual language Seong Ryul has been refining for several years, and arrives with an unusual credential — filmmaker Bong Joon Ho contributed an essay to the accompanying catalogue, describing the unease he finds humming beneath the work's evident sweetness. That tension, between a postcard-pretty surface and the faint sense that everything pictured has already slipped into the past, is what makes the paintings worth lingering over rather than just admiring.

shows.title: Art School: When We Become Each Other's School
shows.description:
This is a show about the alternative schools artists build for themselves once formal art education ends. ARKO Art Center invited eight self-organized collectives, study groups, and studios — Material Library, Mockcamp, Birdcall, Kuroda, Curating School Seoul, Haengbokban, PIE, and YPC × Rat Journal — to lay out how they built their own ongoing "art schools," and the 42 participating artists fill both main galleries with the physical residue of years of informal teaching and learning: reading-group ephemera, workshop notes, study materials, and collaborative pieces produced along the way.

Material Library turns three years of shared research into painting, printmaking, and 3D-scanning materials into a working studio display, while Curating School Seoul collages interview transcripts, objects, and images from dozens of participants into a piece about how learning, care, and survival as an artist are entangled. Other groups built participatory works: PIE hides sentences behind QR codes scattered through the galleries for visitors to hunt down, and YPC × Rat Journal invite viewers to write and bring in their own texts and objects.

Framed as a corrective to the neoliberal pressures on formal art academies, the show treats collectives, alternative spaces, and artist-run study groups not as a fallback but as a parallel and often more sustaining educational system — a timely subject given how much of Seoul's own experimental art scene runs on exactly this kind of self-organization. Around twenty related public programs, from reading clubs to roundtables, run throughout the exhibition's ten-week run.
